meta.description: Not W. H. Auden. This exact epigram is ascribed to Lord Dewar in 1926 newspapers — and the joke was already in print by 1897.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If We Are Here to Help Others, I Often Wonder What the Others Are Here For'?
meta.ogDescription: Auden quoted a different version; Lord Dewar got the credit in 1926. The joke goes back to an 1897 Brookline lecture by a Harvard professor, per Quote Investigator.

answer.label: Not W. H. Auden — ascribed to Lord Dewar
answer.authorDates: 1864–1930 · Scottish whisky distiller, MP and peer
answer.sourceLine: This exact wording is an epigram ascribed to Lord Dewar in 1926 newspaper printings — the fullest being “A Peer’s Epigrams” in the Malayan Saturday Post of 12 June 1926. Auden never wrote this sentence; the line he did use was a different one, and he was knowingly quoting a music-hall comedian. Quote Investigator adds the honest caveat that Dewar “may have used it, but he did not originate it” — the joke was already in print in 1897.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — the popular credit to W. H. Auden is wrong, and even the Dewar ascription is an attribution rather than a proven coinage.

source.excerpt:
Life is full of trials, with an occasional conviction.
We want less artillery rattle and more baby rattles.
If we are here to help others, I often wonder what the others are here for.
—Lord Dewar
trail: 1897 — Harvard professor George Herbert Palmer tells a Brookline audience about two children debating the point of living; the boy’s reply is the punchline. Printed in the society’s Year Book, p. 16 ↗, followed by Palmer’s verdict: “This is the weakness of altruism.”

1923 — the comedian John Foster Hall, as “The Revd. Vivian Foster, the Vicar of Mirth,” delivers the adult version on the record The Parson Addresses His Flock: “We are all here on earth to help others; what on earth the others are here for, I don’t know” — documented by Edward Mendelson ↗.

1926 — the joke appears ascribed to Lord Dewar, first in a looser form in a speech report of 15 March — “If we are to help others, I wonder what the others are here for” — and then in this exact wording in “A Peer’s Epigrams” of 12 June, both cited by Quote Investigator ↗.

1942 and 1948 — Auden borrows Foster Hall’s wording, first in “The Fabian Figaro” (Commonweal, 23 October 1942) and again in “Squares and Oblongs.” He never claims it; the Auden Society lists it among things Auden never wrote ↗.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed by Quote Investigator from the 12 June 1926 Malayan Saturday Post, p. 19, col. 2, via Singapore’s NewspaperSG database. The epigrams around it are the giveaway: this is a dinner-speech wit’s repertoire, not a poet’s line.

source.rightsNote: This wording is documented only in 1926 newspaper printings — the Bradford Daily Telegraph of 15 March 1926 (in a looser variant) and the Malayan Saturday Post of 12 June 1926 — and the underlying joke was in print in the United States from 1897. Everything in that chain was published well before 1931, so the sentence itself is in the public domain in the US, and Lord Dewar died in 1930. Note that Auden’s different wording, as published in Commonweal in 1942 and reprinted since, is a 20th-century text still under copyright — but that is not the sentence quoted here.

author.name: Thomas Robert Dewar, 1st Baron Dewar

author.heading: Who was Lord Dewar?
author.metaLine: 1864–1930 · Scottish whisky distiller, MP and peer · called in 1927 the “King of Epigrammatists”
author.bio: Tommy Dewar (6 January 1864 – 11 April 1930) was the salesman half of the Scottish whisky family that built Dewar’s into an international brand, travelling the world to open new markets while his brother John ran the home office. He sat as an MP from 1900 to 1906, was knighted in 1902, made a baronet in 1917, and created Baron Dewar in 1919. He was also a professional wit: by November 1927 Pearson’s Magazine was collecting “The Witty Sayings of Lord Dewar, King of Epigrammatists” — and this line sat among them.

misattribution.heading: Three names on one joke
misattribution.intro: This quip is one of the most heavily re-credited lines in circulation, and the two famous names attached to it are both later borrowers. Quote Investigator’s own framing of the question notes it “has been attributed to the prominent poet W. H. Auden and the Scottish whisky distiller Thomas Dewar.”

items.why: Auden never wrote this exact sentence. What he wrote — in the essay “The Fabian Figaro” in Commonweal, 23 October 1942, and again in “Squares and Oblongs” in 1948 — was a different wording: “we are all here on earth to help others: what on earth the others are here for, I don’t know.” Wikiquote files a variant of that line — “We are all on earth to help others. What on earth the others are here for, I can’t imagine” — under “Misattributed,” crediting Foster Hall ↗. Quote sites nonetheless run it under his name with no source at all — Goodreads credits it to W. H. Auden with no book given ↗.

items.who: John Foster Hall — “The Revd. Vivian Foster, the Vicar of Mirth”
items.tag: The real source of Auden’s line
items.why: Edward Mendelson of the W. H. Auden Society identifies the sentence Auden used as one spoken by the English music-hall and radio comedian John Foster Hall (1867–1945) on his 1923 recording The Parson Addresses His Flock. Mendelson writes that Auden “never claimed credit for it” and that the real authorship stayed unknown to Auden scholars until 2002 — read the Auden Society note ↗.

items.scope: The exact wording on this page
items.why: Dewar is where this phrasing enters print, in two 1926 newspaper items — a speech reported in the Bradford Daily Telegraph on 15 March 1926 in the variant form “If we are to help others, I wonder what the others are here for,” and the tighter version in “A Peer’s Epigrams” on 12 June 1926. But Quote Investigator is careful: “he may have used it, but he did not originate it” ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The joke outdates all three men. Its earliest known printing is the 1897 Year Book of the Brookline Education Society ↗, where Harvard professor George Herbert Palmer reports two children arguing about the point of living — and the punchline belongs to a small boy.

context.heading: Why this one travels so well
lead: The joke is a logic trap dressed as a platitude. Tell someone their purpose is to serve others, and the obvious question is what job that leaves for the others — altruism eating its own tail. That is exactly how it first appears in print: not as an aphorism at all, but as a child’s objection.

In January 1897 the Harvard philosopher George Herbert Palmer (1842–1933) told a Brookline, Massachusetts audience about two children overheard talking at bedtime. The girl said she was here “to help others”; the boy asked, “Well, what are the others here for?” Palmer’s own gloss follows immediately: “This is the weakness of altruism” ↗. For the next thirty years the gag circulated in newspapers as a nursery exchange — Johnny and Little Sister, Willie and Pa, a clergyman and his son.
context.detailsSummary: How a nursery gag became a poet’s epigram
detailsBody: The polishing happened in two steps. Around 1923 the English music-hall and radio comedian John Foster Hall (1867–1945), performing as “The Revd. Vivian Foster, the Vicar of Mirth,” put it in an adult’s mouth on the record The Parson Addresses His Flock: “We are all here on earth to help others; what on earth the others are here for, I don’t know.” The children are gone; the pulpit does the work.

Three years later a second polish produced the version on this page. Lord Dewar, by then a professional dinner-table wit, was reported delivering it as one epigram among several — “Hope is the undergarment of optimism,” “Life is full of trials, with an occasional conviction.” The tighter, first-person “I often wonder” construction is the one that stuck on quote sites.

Auden comes last, and he comes as a reader. He dropped Foster Hall’s wording into his 1942 essay on Bernard Shaw as a parenthetical aside, and used it again in 1948 in “Squares and Oblongs.” Edward Mendelson notes that Auden never claimed credit for it — but a famous name attached to a good line is hard to detach, and the real source stayed unknown to Auden scholars until a 2002 letter in The Spectator identified it.
context.pull: It started as a child’s objection, became a comedian’s catchphrase, and only then acquired famous authors.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator documents the exact wording "If we are here to help others, I often wonder what the others are here for" in "A Peer's Epigrams," Malayan Saturday Post (Singapore), 12 June 1926, p. 19, col. 2, ascribed to Lord Dewar; documents an earlier Dewar variant in the Bradford Daily Telegraph of 15 March 1926 ("If we are to help others, I wonder what the others are here for"); traces the earliest printing of the joke to the 1897 Year Book of the Brookline Education Society (George Herbert Palmer, p. 16); records Auden's use of a DIFFERENT wording in "The Fabian Figaro," Commonweal, 23 October 1942, and in "Squares and Oblongs" (1948); and concludes Dewar "may have used it, but he did not originate it" and that Auden "did employ the quip more than once, but it was already in circulation."

Edward Mendelson, on the W. H. Auden Society site, attributes the line Auden used to John Foster Hall (1867-1945), performing as "The Revd. Vivian Foster, the Vicar of Mirth," on a 1923 recording titled "The Parson Addresses His Flock"; gives the wording as "We are all here on earth to help others; what on earth the others are here for, I don't know"; states Auden "never claimed credit for it" and that the real authorship remained unknown to Auden scholars until 2002; and identifies Auden's first use as a review in The Commonweal, 23 October 1942.

The W. H. Auden Society's page "A Few Things Auden Never Wrote," by Edward Mendelson, includes the "We are all here on earth to help others" line among items Auden is commonly credited with but did not originate, crediting it instead to John Foster Hall.

Wikiquote's W. H. Auden page lists "We are all on earth to help others. What on earth the others are here for, I can't imagine." under the section heading "Misattributed," noting the quotation has been traced to John Foster Hall (1867-1945), an English comedian known as "The Reverend Vivian Foster, Vicar of Mirth," citing Edward Mendelson at audensociety.org.

Google Books full view of the Year Book of the Brookline Education Society (1897) contains, on the page indexed as p. 16, the text "...others here for?" followed by "This is the weakness of altruism." — Palmer's anecdote of two children.

Wikipedia records Thomas Dewar, 1st Baron Dewar as born 6 January 1864 in Perth, Scotland and died 11 April 1930; Scottish whisky distiller and businessman; Member of Parliament 1900-1906; knighted 1902; baronet 1917; created Baron Dewar 1919.

Goodreads presents "We are all here on earth to help others: what on earth the others are here for, I don't know." credited to W.H. Auden with no source work given — evidence of the ongoing popular misattribution.
